clue.text: Comrades almost chucked in firearm

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter of the word is dropped
in places the shortened word inside the name of the gun

blocks.note: the Bren is a British light machine gun
chucked means tossed; its last letter goes

explanation.surface: Fellow soldiers have nearly thrown their weapons into a heap.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bren gun is a standard crossword firearm; the shortened word goes into it, splitting it after its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Brethren is an old plural of brother, used for fellow members of a group or society, much like comrades.

clue.text: Part of England Scots understood

blocks.note: first meaning: a county in the south-east
second meaning: the Scottish past tense of ken, to know

explanation.surface: A region of England that people in Scotland grasped.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scots, ken means to know and its past form is kent; Kent is also an English county south-east of London.
explanation.definitionFit: The county is a southeastern region of the country, while the Scots verb form means knew or grasped.

clue.text: Detective returns to familiar territory in hearing

indicators.note: in hearing tells us the word is judged by how it strikes the ear, not its spelling

blocks.note: a pigeon or missile homes when it returns to a known place

explanation.surface: A sleuth goes back over familiar ground in a court hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: The L in the famous name is silent, so it is pronounced like homes.
explanation.definitionFit: Sherlock Holmes is Conan Doyle's fictional consulting detective, the archetype of the brilliant investigator.

clue.text: Otherwise learnt outside University, unlike 15 or 17

indicators.note: otherwise means in another manner, so the letters are set out differently
outside means the rearranged letters wrap around the abbreviation

blocks.note: the letters of learnt reordered
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: Something learnt off campus, contrasted with two other entries.
explanation.walkthrough: NE(U)TRAL. Entries 15 and 17 are ENEMIES and FRIENDS, so the answer is someone who is neither.
explanation.definitionFit: A neutral party takes no side, being neither hostile foe nor supportive ally to anyone.

clue.text: Affectionate type picking me up with Dutch courage

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written, then turned round
Dutch courage is drink-fuelled bravery; a bracer is a stiffening drink

explanation.surface: A cuddly person offers a pick-me-up drink for courage.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface hides the phrase pick-me-up, itself a word for a tonic drink, which makes the drink reading feel natural.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who embraces hugs people warmly, so an embracer is an affectionate, demonstrative person.

clue.text: Reveal city must be reconstructed in original way

indicators.note: reconstructed means built again in a new form, so the letters are reassembled

blocks.note: the fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: An urban planner explains how a city should be rebuilt imaginatively.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something creatively means using imagination and invention, making it fresh rather than copied.

clue.text: Concrete help for teaching about others

blocks.note: re means concerning, as in a business letter
alia is Latin for other things, as in inter alia

explanation.surface: Practical support for teachers dealing with other people.
explanation.walkthrough: Realia are real objects brought into a classroom; concrete here means tangible, not cement.
explanation.definitionFit: In education, realia are physical everyday objects used as teaching aids, a tangible kind of classroom support.

clue.text: Regret nothing after short time, sweetheart

indicators.note: after places the regret-and-nothing part second, behind the short time piece

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
to rue is to regret
love is zero in tennis scoring

explanation.surface: A lover feels no remorse after a brief fling.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is read in reverse clue order: T comes first, then RUE and LOVE.
explanation.definitionFit: A true-love is an old poetic term for a beloved person or darling.

clue.text: Expert solver of clues needs extra, consuming seconds

indicators.note: consuming means swallowing up, so one word takes the other inside it

blocks.note: more means additional
S is the abbreviation for seconds

explanation.surface: A crossword champion wants more, eating up second helpings.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Morse, the Oxford TV detective, was a keen crossword solver, so clues works both ways.
explanation.definitionFit: Inspector Morse is a fictional Oxford detective who solves crime clues and loves cryptic crosswords.

clue.text: Take part in taste test, etc. sooner or later? Don’t touch it

indicators.note: taking part of a phrase means lifting a run of letters out of it
says the run of letters can be found at an earlier spot or a later spot in the clue

blocks.note: the letters sit across the two words
surface padding here; with the word before it, it offers the same run of letters a second time

explanation.surface: A food sampler is told to keep off the dishes being judged.
explanation.walkthrough: The hidden word appears earlier (taSTE Test) and again later (teST ETc), hence sooner or later. STET is a proofreader's mark meaning leave as it was.
explanation.definitionFit: Stet is Latin for let it stand, an editor's instruction to leave text unchanged.

clue.text: King and I protected by partners in terms of wealth

indicators.note: something protected by others is surrounded by them

blocks.note: first partner: a mate
R is short for Rex, king
taken as written
second partner: an ally

explanation.surface: The musical The King and I, with its star guarded by companions.
explanation.walkthrough: Partners is plural, so it supplies two separate words that sit either side of the king and the I.
explanation.definitionFit: Materially means in respect of money and possessions, as in being materially better off.

clue.text: Far from sweet superpower, onetime ally turned deadly foe

blocks.note: brut describes very dry champagne
the United States

explanation.surface: A sour superpower ditches an old partner and becomes an enemy.
explanation.walkthrough: Brutus was Caesar's friend who joined the assassins.
explanation.definitionFit: Brutus was a close associate of Julius Caesar who then helped stab him, the classic betraying friend.

clue.text: Corporation showed sign of cut – admit it’s in very bad shape

blocks.note: corporation is old slang for a pot belly
a cut bleeds
to own up is to admit

explanation.surface: A company revealed a spending cut and confessed it was struggling.
explanation.walkthrough: Corporation is a jokey old word for a large belly, hence TUM.
explanation.definitionFit: A tumbledown building is dilapidated and falling apart, which is being in very poor condition.

clue.text: Chapter penned by a competitor relating to record collection

indicators.note: something penned by others is shut inside them, like an animal in a fold

blocks.note: a rival is a competitor
CH is the abbreviation for chapter

explanation.surface: A competing author writes a chapter about collecting vinyl records.
explanation.walkthrough: Record collection suggests vinyl, but here it means a store of documents.
explanation.definitionFit: Archives are collections of historical documents and records, so archival concerns that kind of storage.

clue.text: Bad men I see?

indicators.note: bad means spoiled or faulty, so the following letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: Someone spots villains approaching and wonders who they are.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: the villains someone spots are their foes.
explanation.definitionFit: Enemies are hostile opponents, people viewed as bad from one's own side.

clue.text: Stylized language I use with umph, bizarrely

indicators.note: bizarrely means in a strange way, so the letters come out in an odd order

blocks.note: taken as fodder
taken as fodder

explanation.surface: A writer admits using ornate phrasing with oomph, oddly.
explanation.walkthrough: The term comes from Lyly's Euphues, an Elizabethan prose romance.
explanation.definitionFit: Euphuism is an artificial, highly elaborate prose manner, full of antithesis and alliteration.

clue.text: Run into fanatics, members of religious society

indicators.note: into means going inside, so the letter is placed within the word

blocks.note: a fiend is an enthusiast, as in fitness fiend
R is the cricket abbreviation for a run

explanation.surface: Bumping into zealots who belong to a church.
explanation.walkthrough: FI(R)ENDS. The Religious Society of Friends is the formal name of the Quakers.
explanation.definitionFit: Quakers call themselves Friends, belonging to the Religious Society of Friends.

clue.text: Set off with girlfriend outside boys’ school

indicators.note: outside means one word wraps around the other

blocks.note: a date is someone you are going out with
Eton is the famous English boys' public school

explanation.surface: A schoolboy heads out with his girlfriend, meeting outside the school gates.
explanation.walkthrough: D(ETON)ATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To set off a bomb or explosive charge is to make it explode, triggering it.

clue.text: Hiding name, discharge Brendan’s buddy? Not always

indicators.note: a word that is hiding something holds it inside

blocks.note: to discharge a prisoner is to set them at liberty
N is the abbreviation for name
Brendan is the setter, so his possessive from his own mouth is my

explanation.surface: The setter keeps quiet about who his sometime pal is.
explanation.walkthrough: FRE(N)E + MY. Brendan is the setter, so Brendan's means my.
explanation.definitionFit: A frenemy is someone who acts as a friend but is also a rival, so only sometimes a pal.

clue.text: Striker’s corrupt power ensnaring everyone

indicators.note: corrupt means debased or spoiled, so the letters are scrambled
ensnaring means catching and holding, so one part goes inside the other

blocks.note: the letters of power rearranged
all means everyone

explanation.surface: A footballer's crooked influence traps the whole team.
explanation.walkthrough: W(ALL)OPER. Striker suggests a footballer, but here it is someone who hits hard; walloper is British slang, also for a policeman in Scotland and Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: To wallop is to hit hard, so a walloper is one who strikes or thumps.

clue.text: Learner in a sport becoming top Olympian

indicators.note: in means the letter sits inside the phrase

blocks.note: polo is a sport played on horseback
L is the learner-driver plate

explanation.surface: A novice at a game rises to become a champion at the Olympics.
explanation.walkthrough: Olympian suggests an athlete, but it means a god of Mount Olympus.
explanation.definitionFit: Apollo was one of the chief gods dwelling on Mount Olympus, so a leading deity there.

clue.text: Wild dog you almost trapped in sheep pen

indicators.note: almost means not completely, so the last letter is lost
trapped in means held inside the enclosure

blocks.note: a cote is a shelter for sheep or doves
taken as written, then shortened

explanation.surface: A wild canine has very nearly been caught among the sheep.
explanation.walkthrough: A cote is a small shelter for animals, usually doves or sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: The coyote is a wolf-like canine of North America, a wild relative of the domestic dog.

clue.text: A doctor finally got in antidote for poison

indicators.note: finally points to the end letter of the word before it
got in means entered, so these letters go inside the other word

blocks.note: a cure is a remedy
taken as written
the final letter of doctor

explanation.surface: A physician finally gets the antidote in to treat a poisoning.
explanation.walkthrough: The inserted pair goes in near the end of the remedy word, just before its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Curare is a plant extract used by South American hunters on arrow tips, paralysing prey.

clue.text: Central American native reportedly went on racehorse

indicators.note: reportedly means as spoken by others, so the word is chosen for its sound

blocks.note: rowed means travelled on water by oar
a horse in a race is a runner

explanation.surface: An indigenous Central American is said to have backed a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: Native suggests a person, but it is a bird found in Mexico and the south-western US.
explanation.definitionFit: The roadrunner is a fast-running ground cuckoo native to Mexico and the American south-west.

clue.text: Length once more uncompleted in part of pool

indicators.note: uncompleted means unfinished, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for length
anew means again

explanation.surface: A swimmer does yet another length, never quite finishing, in the pool.
explanation.walkthrough: L + ANE(W).
explanation.definitionFit: A swimming pool is divided by ropes into lanes, strips along which swimmers race.

clue.text: King Edward the humorist

blocks.note: first meaning: Shakespeare's tragic monarch
second meaning: the Victorian writer of nonsense verse

explanation.walkthrough: King Edward looks like a monarch's name, but the clue splits after King.
explanation.definitionFit: King Lear is Shakespeare's tragedy, and Edward Lear wrote limericks and The Owl and the Pussy-cat.

clue.text: Oxford writer in North Island

blocks.note: first meaning: C. S. ..., Oxford academic and author of Narnia
second meaning: the northern part of ... and Harris in the Outer Hebrides

explanation.surface: An Oxford author is staying on an island in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: North Island suggests New Zealand, but it is the Hebridean island off north-west Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: C. S. Lewis taught at Oxford, and Lewis is the largest island in Scotland's Outer Hebrides.

clue.text: Master criminal orchestrated army riot

indicators.note: orchestrated means arranged, so the following letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A criminal mastermind stirred up a mutiny among the troops.
explanation.definitionFit: Professor Moriarty is Sherlock Holmes's archenemy, called the Napoleon of crime by Conan Doyle.
